newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan, China to hold talks on direct links - report.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan, China to hold talks on direct links - report.

text.p: Shipping executives from Taiwan and China will meet in Hong Kong in October to discuss direct links between the island and the mainland, local newspapers reported on Tuesday.

Both sides were also expected to discuss the status of shipping links between Taiwan and Hong Kong after the British colony's mid-1997 handover to Chinese sovereignty, the papers quoted Lin Hsing-shan, head of a private Taiwan group trying to end a ban on direct links with China, as saying.
The talks would be held by Lin's group and a mainland counterpart, but transport officials from Taipei and Beijing would participate in their private capacity, the reports said.
Lin was quoted as saying the two sides hoped to sign an agreement during the meeting and establish links between Taiwan ports and the mainland cities of Xiamen and Fuzhou by the end of 1996.
Lin returned to Taipei on Monday from China after meeting senior Chinese transport officials and shipping executives.
He told local media that the atmosphere was good during his China visit and Chinese authorities said the links should be established as soon as possible.
Lin was not immediately available for comment.

To fulfil its ambition of becoming a regional hub, Taiwan proposed in 1995 to set up an offshore transshipment centre at its southern Kaohsiung port from which ships would be allowed to sail directly across the Taiwan Strait.
The project has been delayed by sovereignty issues.

On August 20, China unveiled rules governing direct shipping links across the Strait, effective immediately, but Taiwan gave a cool response, saying Beijing's rules were "mingled with sensitive political issues".

China's regulations allow wholly Chinese-owned or Taiwan-owned shipping companies or joint ventures involving Chinese or Taiwanese shipowners to sail between the two sides. Taiwan insists on the transshipment centre.
Taiwan has banned direct air and shipping links with China since Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists lost the civil war to the communists and fled to the island in 1949.
With tensions easing since the late 1980s, civilian aircraft and vessels have skirted the ban by stopping over in Hong Kong, Macau or elsewhere.
Taiwan investors, who have poured more than $20 billion into China, have pressured the government to establish such links to save transport costs.
